title.en: The First Day: Finding the Planet

text.en: The Elohim, “those who came from the sky”, began their work on a new world: searching space for the planet best suited to their project, they found the Earth.

The Earth then lay entirely under water and thick mists. Above the waters the Elohim carried out reconnaissance trips and placed what might be called artificial satellites around the planet to study its makeup and its atmosphere.

The Elohim then studied the sunlight reaching the surface, since life could not be created there if the sun sent harmful rays. It warmed the Earth correctly without them, and the light was judged good.
So ended the first “day” of the work: the period during which the sun rises under the same sign on the day of the spring equinox, about two thousand Earth years.
The subject of the first verse is *Elohim*, a Hebrew word plural in form. When it names the God of Israel it usually takes singular verbs, as it does with *bara* here.

The Messages say the word was unjustly translated in some Bibles as “God”: it means “those who came from the sky” and it is indeed plural. The Elohim are scientists from another planet who had learned to create primitive forms of life, living cells in test tubes, until public opinion and the government of their planet forbade the experiments. They left for a distant planet that met just about all their conditions, and chose the Earth.
The gloss “those who came from the sky” is the canon’s own rendering and is not the consensus etymology, which derives the word through *Eloah* and *El*.

In the Messages’ reading, the verse’s “created” means “in reality discovered”. The scientists looked for the planet most suitable for their projects and found that the Earth held every element needed to create artificial life, although its atmosphere was not quite identical to their own.

The first word, *bereshit*, has no article and can be read as a construct, “in the beginning of …”; many modern translations follow this with “When … began to create”, while others keep “In the beginning”. The Wheel of Heaven translation reads “When the Elohim began to shape”.
That temporal reading suits the Messages’ account, in which the work begins on a planet that already exists.

In the Messages’ account, the Earth at this point was covered entirely by water and thick mists. The Messages quote “the Spirit of Elohim moved upon the face of the waters” and follow the quotation at once with the Elohim’s reconnaissance: survey trips, and “what you might call artificial satellites” placed around the Earth to study its makeup and its atmosphere.
The Messages do not equate the two in so many words; reading the hovering “breath” as the survey itself is an inference from where the comment stands.

The Hebrew *ruach* means wind, breath or spirit, and *merachefet* describes a hovering or fluttering motion, used of an eagle over its young in Deuteronomy 32:11. The Wheel of Heaven translation renders the phrase “the breath of the Elohim hovering”.

The light that “was good” is sunlight. Before creating life, the Elohim had to know whether the sun sent harmful rays to the surface. Their study showed that it warmed the Earth correctly without them.

These studies took a long time. The Messages define the “day” as the period during which the sun rises under the same sign on the day of the spring equinox: about two thousand Earth years. Each “day” of Genesis 1 is one long stage of the creation work, and “evening and morning” closes each stage.

The canon’s definition is that of a precessional age. The Wheel of Heaven timeline goes one step further: it gives each day the model length of about 2,160 years and assigns the days to named ages in sequence. The canon’s own round figure, about two thousand years, is the one this reading follows.

alt.en: Diagram of the six creation days as successive working stages of about two thousand years each: the survey of the planet and its light; the work beneath the clouds; the single continent and the first plants; the study of the sky; life in the seas and the air; land animals and humankind.

title.en: The Second Day: Beneath the Clouds

text.en: The Elohim turned to the layer of air between two bodies of water: the clouds above and the ocean below.
After studying the cosmic radiation above the clouds, they came down beneath the cloud cover and worked there, between the waters above and the ocean that covered the whole Earth.
That space beneath the clouds they called the skies, and a second period of work, again about two thousand years, came to an end.

The Messages quote the separation of “the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament” and read it as a description of where the Elohim were working. Having studied cosmic radiation above the clouds, they descended below the clouds while remaining above the water. The waters above are the clouds; the waters below are the ocean, which still covered the whole Earth.

The Hebrew *raqia*, rendered “dome” in the Wheel of Heaven translation, comes from a verb meaning to hammer out a metal sheet. Ancient Near Eastern cosmology pictured a solid vault holding back the upper waters.
Read as a working report, the same vocabulary describes what observers between cloud and sea would see: a band of air with water above it and water below it.
In the Hebrew text the second day is the only one without the formula “the Elohim saw that it was good”; the Greek Septuagint supplies it.

The Messages’ sequence suggests a reason. The work beneath the clouds leads straight into the next stage, the study of the ocean floor and the raising of the land, so the verdict waits for the third day, where it comes twice (1:10, 1:12). Rashi gave a similar explanation: the work on the waters was not finished until the third day.

title.en: The Third Day: One Continent and the First Plants

text.en: The Elohim studied the sea floor, found it shallow and roughly level everywhere, and with powerful explosions piled material from the seabed into one place until dry land rose above the water.
The land they raised formed a single continent, surrounded by the gathered seas, and the Elohim judged the work good.
On this continent, now a vast laboratory, the Elohim created plant cells from chemical substances alone, and from them plants of every kind, each designed above all to reproduce itself.

Research teams spread across the continent, each creating different plants according to its climate and its inspiration, and artists joined them to make some plants purely beautiful in shape or scent.
So closed the third period of work, another span of about two thousand years.

After studying the surface of the oceans, the Elohim studied the sea floor and found it shallow and roughly even everywhere. Using fairly powerful explosions, which did something like the work of bulldozers, they removed material from the bottom of the seas and gathered it in one place. This formed a continent. According to the Messages the Earth at first had only one continent, and scientists had recently realised that the continents, which later drifted apart, fit together into a single one.
Mainstream geology calls the former supercontinent Pangaea and dates the start of its breakup to about 200 million years ago.
In the Messages’ account of the Flood, “the continent was submerged by an immense tidal wave that destroyed all life on its surface”.

The Messages say the continents later drifted apart but do not say when. The Wheel of Heaven reading dates the breakup to the Flood strike (see Genesis 7); that dating comes from Marcel Terrusse’s essay printed in *Let’s Welcome the Extraterrestrials*, not from the dictated Messages, which still speak of “the whole continent” at Babel.

On this “magnificent and gigantic laboratory” the Elohim created plant cells from nothing other than chemical products, and from them plants of all kinds. Their effort went above all into reproduction: the first blades of grass they brought into being had to be able to reproduce.
The verse’s repeated “according to its kind”, with the seed carried inside the plant, matches that concern: each design reproduces true to type.

The scientists spread over the continent in separate research groups, each creating different plants according to its climate and its inspiration, and they met at regular intervals to compare their work. Their home planet followed it with wonder, and its finest artists came to give some plants a purely decorative purpose, through their appearance or their fragrance.

title.en: The Fourth Day: Reading the Sky

text.en: The Elohim then studied the lights of the sky, the sun and the stars, as markers that divide day from night and count out the days and years of the Earth.
These lights, shining on the land, gave them their bearings on the new planet.
They charted the greater light that governs the day, the lesser light that governs the night, and the stars.
By these lights the Elohim measured the Earth’s days, months and years, quite unlike those of their home planet, and regulated their lives by them; the work was judged good.
A fourth period of work came to an end.

By observing the stars and the sun, the Elohim measured the length of days, months and years on Earth. These measures helped them regulate their lives on a planet so different from their own, where neither the days nor the years had the same length. Astronomical study also let them locate themselves exactly and come to know the Earth better.

The Messages already have the sun warming the Earth on the first day, so the luminaries that the Elohim “make” and “set” in the sky here are best read as lights they charted and put to use as a calendar.

Genesis avoids the ordinary Hebrew words for sun and moon, *shemesh* and *yareach*, and names them only by function, the greater and the lesser luminary. It calls them *otot*, signs, and *moadim*, appointed times.
That functional, calendrical vocabulary suits a compressed report of people measuring time on a new world.

In English and French the “signs” of verse 14 echo the canon’s own unit for a creation day, the sign under which the sun rises at the spring equinox. The Hebrew *otot* means signs or marks in general, so the echo depends on the translation.

title.en: The Fifth Day: Life in the Seas and the Air

text.en: The Elohim created the first life in the waters, from plankton to small fish and then very large fish, and balanced it so that each species had food without wiping out another.
After the fish came the birds, which the artists covered in wild colours and astonishing shapes, while other teams made appalling creatures: dragons, “or what you have named Dinosaurs”.

The Elohim meant the sea creatures and the birds to breed and fill their domains, and the competing teams went as far as reshaping the birds’ behaviour before mating into ever more admirable courtship dances.
A fifth period of work came to an end.

The Elohim next created the first aquatic animals: plankton, then small fish, then very large fish. So that this living world would stay in balance, they created algae for the small fish to feed on and large fish to eat the smaller ones, so that no species would completely destroy another it needed for food. The Messages call it, in a way, what is now called ecology, and the work succeeded.

The teams often met and held competitions to name the group that had created the most beautiful or most interesting animal. After the fish they created the birds, under pressure from the artists, who gave them the wildest colours and the most astonishing shapes, sometimes with decorative feathers so cumbersome that the birds could scarcely fly. The competitions went further still: the scientists modified the birds’ behaviour before mating so that their courtship dances became ever more admirable.
The Messages do not comment on the blessing of verse 22, “be fruitful and multiply”. Setting it beside the courtship dances, which concern pairing and breeding, is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

The Messages return to this point elsewhere: no natural need explains the birds’ blue or red feathers, their “amorous demonstrations” or the spiral horns of certain antelopes, which are the work of the creators’ “artists”.
Other teams created appalling animals, monsters that proved right those at home who had opposed the experiments: “Dragons, or what you have named Dinosaurs or Brontosaurs, and so on.”

Verse 21’s *tanninim*, “great sea creatures” in most English versions and “great dragons” in the Wheel of Heaven translation, after Dhorme’s *grands dragons*, is the Hebrew Bible’s word for sea monsters and serpent-dragons (Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:13).

The Messages quote verses 20 and 24 and pass over verse 21, yet the narrative between those quotations supplies its dragons at this very stage. The corpus reads this as a report telling its own story without leaning on its best proof-text; the plainer explanation is that the Messages quote only the command that opens each stage.

title.en: The Sixth Day: Land Animals and Humankind

text.en: On a continent whose vegetation had grown magnificent, the Elohim created land animals, the plant-eaters first, since there was food for them.
They then made meat-eaters to keep the plant-eaters in balance, so that here too the species would keep one another in check.
Then the most skilled among the Elohim set out to create, artificially, human beings like themselves, in their own image, to have charge of the creatures of sea, sky and land.
Each team made its humans in the Elohim’s likeness, male and female. The Messages note that “the resemblance is striking”, and each human race corresponds to a team of creators.
The Elohim set their new humans the same course as the sea creatures and birds of the fifth day: to breed, spread across the land and hold sway over the creatures of sea, sky and land.

For food the creators assigned the first humans the seed-bearing plants and the fruit of the trees; the verse gives the green plants to the animals as well, a grant the Messages, which have the creators make meat-eaters, do not take up.
The Elohim looked over all their work and judged it very good. So closed the sixth period of work, about two thousand years like the others.

After the seas and the air, the Elohim created land animals on a continent whose vegetation had become magnificent. The herbivores came first, since there was food for them; carnivores followed to balance the herbivore population, so that here too the species would keep one another in check. The speaker of the Messages, Yahweh, says that these men came from his planet and that he is one of those who created life on Earth.

Then the most skilled among the Elohim wanted to create, artificially, a human being like themselves. Each team set to work, and the results were soon compared. On their home planet these “test-tube children” caused a scandal: people feared that the new humans might become a danger if their abilities turned out to be greater than their creators’. The creators had to commit to letting them live primitively, revealing nothing scientific to them and mystifying their own actions. The number of teams can still be read in humanity: each human race corresponds to one team of creators.

*Na’aseh*, “let us make”, is a first-person plural, and “our image” and “our likeness” are plural as well. Verse 27 returns to a singular verb and a singular suffix (*betsalmo*, “in his image”); the Wheel of Heaven translation renders that verse in the plural, in keeping with its plural Elohim.
The Messages read the plural as the creators speaking of themselves, and comment on “in our image” that the resemblance is striking.

They also explain the sequence that evolutionary theory describes as the progress of the creators’ techniques: they began with very simple organisms and went on to make “the fish, the batrachians, the mammals, the birds, the primates, and finally man”, a model of improved monkey to which they added what made them human. The skulls of prehistoric humans are early prototypes, supplanted by more advanced types until the human became the exact replica of its creators.

That list names the birds after the mammals, while the Messages’ own creation account (TBWTT 2:22–24) has the birds made straight after the fish and before any land animal, the order Genesis 1 also follows. The Messages do not reconcile the two sequences.
The Messages do not comment on this passage; what follows is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

The blessing of verse 28 repeats to humankind the charge given to the sea creatures and birds on the fifth day, to multiply and fill their domain. Read through the canon, it states the creators’ design for a new population meant to spread across the land.
The food grant of verses 29–30 gives plants alone, to humans and animals alike. Permission to eat meat comes only after the Flood (Genesis 9:3).
This sits uneasily with the Messages’ account, in which large fish eat smaller ones and carnivores were created to balance the herbivores.

One Wheel of Heaven reading takes the grant as the diet set for the first humans and the animals kept near them in the creators’ care, leaving the predators of the wider world outside its view. Nothing in the canon states this.
Verse 31 closes the creation work with “very good”. Of the six days, the Hebrew gives only this one the article, “the sixth day”, balancing the cardinal “day one” that opened the sequence.
In the Messages’ reckoning it ends the last of six working periods, each about two thousand Earth years long.
